Although a daily chromium intake of 200 nanograms/kg has been suggested in children given total parenteral nutrition (TPN), a study in 15 children1 given long- term parenteral nutrition found that supplementation at about this level was associated with serum-chromium concentrations 4 to 42 times higher than the mean value in 15 children not receiving TPN. Raised serum-chromium concentrations were associated with a decrease in glomerular filtration rate; one year after stop- ping chromium supplementation, which reduced intake to 50 nanograms/kg daily (as contaminants of water and TPN solu- tions), chromium concentrations, although lower, were still high- er than controls and renal function had not altered.
